title: At someone's home
goal: Be a good guest (and host) in a Sindhi home: take your shoes off, refuse and accept food the right way, offer to help, stay the night — and talk about how things used to be.
intro:
Sooner or later a friend will say **اسان وٽ اچ** 'come over to ours' — and in Sindh that means tea, then food, then more food, and quite possibly a bed for the night. This unit is about what happens inside the house: the polite back-and-forth of **offering and refusing** (تڪلف نه ڪريو! — تڪلف ڪهڙو!), asking **'should I…?'** (جتيون لاهيان؟ ٿانوَ ڌوئان؟), helping with the chores, and sleeping under a Sindhi **رلي**.

Older relatives love to tell you how things were: **اڳي** 'in the old days' we **رهندا هئاسين** 'used to live'… — so the main new grammar is **'used to'**.

grammar.title: 'Used to': -ndo + هو
grammar.body:
For things that happened **regularly in the past** — habits, routines, 'how things were' — Sindhi takes the **-ndo** participle (the same stem you know from the future: ويندو، رهندو، ڪندو) and adds the **past of 'to be'** (Unit 16). Both parts agree with the subject:

مان ويندو **هوس** vendo hos (m) / ويندي **هيس** vendī huyas (f) — I used to go
هو ويندو **هو** vendo ho / هوءَ ويندي **هئي** vendī huī — he / she used to go
اسين ويندا **هئاسين** vendā huāsīṃ — we used to go
توهان ويندا **هئا** vendā huā — you used to go
هو ويندا **هئا** / وينديون **هيون** vendyūṃ huyūṃ — they used to go

The -ndo forms are built exactly like the future: ڏسندو ɗisando, رهندو rahando, کائيندو khāīndo, and the irregulars ڪندو kando, ايندو endo, ويندو vendo, ڏيندو ɗīndo, هوندو hundo.

For transitive verbs there is **no ergative** here — it's a habitual form, so the subject stays as it is: **مان** چانهه پيئندو هوس (not مون). This is one of the nicest things about 'used to' in Sindhi.

**There used to be** = **هوندو هو / هوندي هئي**: اڳي هتي هڪ دڪان هوندو هو. **Negative**: نه before the verb: مان گوشت نه کائيندو هوس 'I didn't use to eat meat'.

Signal words: **اڳي** 'in the old days', **ننڍپڻ ۾** 'as a child', **روز**، **هر سال**، **هميشه**.

grammar.title: Offering, insisting and declining
grammar.body:
Food in a Sindhi home comes with a little ritual, and knowing your lines makes you a perfect guest.

**1. The host offers** — with a plain polite imperative or a 'shall I?' question: چانهه پيئو · ماني کائو · چانهه ٺاهيان؟

**2. The guest declines (at least once)**: **تڪلف نه ڪريو** 'don't go to any trouble' · **نه مهرباني** · **بس، ڪافي آهي** · اسين کائي آيا آهيون 'we've already eaten'. Saying yes straight away isn't rude, but declining first is the done thing — especially with older people.

**3. The host insists**: **تڪلف ڪهڙو!** 'what trouble!' · **شرم نه ڪريو** 'don't be shy' · and the key word **ته** after the thing offered, meaning **'at least'**: **ٿورو ته** کائو! 'at least have a little!', چانهه **ته** پيئو! 'at least have tea!'. **ڀلا** at the start makes it coaxing: ڀلا هڪ ٻي ماني!

**4. The guest gives in gracefully**: **چڱو، ٿورو** 'OK, a little' · چڱو، **اڌ** پيالو 'OK, half a cup'. When you've truly had enough, say it with a hand over the plate: **بس، هاڻي ٻيو ڪجهه نه** — and if they still insist, a smile and **پيٽ ڀرجي ويو** 'I'm full' ends it.

With close friends the same ritual happens in the intimate form, faster and with more teasing: کاءُ يار، شرم نه ڪر!

examples.en: Please don't trouble yourself — we've already eaten.

grammar.title: 'Should I…?' and 'shall I…?'
grammar.body:
A guest asks a lot of small questions: where to sit, whether shoes come off, whether to help. Sindhi asks them with the **subjunctive** — the present form **without ٿو** (Unit 18):

جتيون **لاهيان**؟ lāhyāṃ — should I take my shoes off?
ڪٿي **ويهان**؟ vehāṃ — where shall I sit?
ٿانوَ **ڌوئان**؟ dhoāṃ — shall I wash the dishes?
اسين اندر **اچون**؟ achūṃ — shall we come in?
مان **ڇا ڪريان**؟ karyāṃ — what should I do?

The endings are: **-āṃ** (I), **-ūṃ** (we). After a vowel stem a **-y-** appears: ڪريان، لاهيان، ٺاهيان.

For **'should' as advice** ('is it right / expected that I…') use the infinitive + **گهرجي** (Unit 9): ڇا مون کي ڪجهه **آڻڻ گهرجي**؟ 'should I bring something?', مون کي ڇا **پائڻ گهرجي**؟ 'what should I wear?'. And to ask what's *required*, use the -ṇo form: جتيون **لاهڻيون** آهن؟ 'do shoes have to come off?' (agreeing with جتيون f pl).

The answer to an offer of help is almost always **نه نه، توهان مهمان آهيو!** — offer once more, then let it go. Among friends, though, a real **هٿ ونڊائڻ** 'lending a hand' is welcome.

examples.roman: moṃ khe shādīa te chhā pāiṇu ghurje?
examples.en: What should I wear to the wedding?

dialogue.setting: Latifabad, Hyderabad. Sarah arrives at her friend Marvi's family home to stay the weekend. Marvi talks to Sarah informally; her mother uses polite forms with the guest at first.

lines.en: Thank you so much, auntie. It feels like I'm in my own home.

culture:
**Guests are a blessing** in Sindhi culture — the old saying is that a guest brings their own luck — and hospitality is serious. Never arrive empty-handed: a box of **مٺائي** (sweets) or fruit is normal. Shoes usually come off at the door of rooms with carpets or where people sit on the floor; if you're not sure, ask **جتيون لاهيان؟** or watch what the family does.

**Refuse first, then accept.** Hosts will offer more than once and insist (**تڪلف ڪهڙو!**, **ٿورو ته کائو!**), and your plate will be refilled the moment it's empty. Leave a little on the plate when you've really had enough. Call your friend's parents **امان** and **بابا** (or **چاچا / ماسي**), not by name — and stand up when an older person comes into the room.

In villages and old family houses men are received in the **اوطاق**, a separate guest room or building where they sit, eat, talk late and often sleep; women visit inside the house. Offering to help with **ٿانوَ** or the **ڪم ڪار** will be refused on a first visit — the refusal is part of the kindness — but by the third visit, pitching in is a sign you've become family. Staying the night is normal, even in the same city, and you'll be given the best **بسترو** and a **رلي**. Leaving takes time: expect a slow goodbye at the door and **ايندڙ ڀيري اسان وٽ اچجو** — which you should answer with an invitation of your own.

tip.title: Should I…? Shall we…?
tip.body:
- Ask with the present form **without ٿو**: جتيون **لاهيان**؟ ڪٿي **ويهان**؟
- 'We': اندر **اچون**؟ ٻاهر **ويهون**؟
- For 'should' as advice use infinitive + **گهرجي**: ڪجهه **آڻڻ گهرجي**؟

tip.title: The offer–refuse–insist dance
tip.body:
- Guest: **تڪلف نه ڪريو** · **نه مهرباني** — refuse once first.
- Host: **تڪلف ڪهڙو!** · **ٿورو ته** کائو! — ته after a word = 'at least'.
- Give in gracefully: **چڱو، ٿورو** · **اڌ** پيالو.
- Really full: **بس، هاڻي ٻيو ڪجهه نه**.

tip.body:
- Offer with the subjunctive: ٿانوَ **ڌوئان**؟ ٻهاري **ڏيان**؟ مان به هٿ **ونڊايان**؟
- 'What should I do?' = مان **ڇا ڪريان؟**
- Expect **نه نه، توهان مهمان آهيو!** — offer once more, then let it go.

tip.title: Sleep comes to you
tip.body:
- 'To fall asleep' is **ننڊ اچڻ** — sleep comes *to* you, so: **مون کي** ننڊ نٿي اچي 'I can't sleep'.
- ننڊ is feminine: ننڊ **آئي**، ننڊ **نٿي** اچي.
- Caring -ijo requests: **جاڳائجو** 'do wake me', **سمهجو** 'do get some sleep'.

sentences.en: Do you need another pillow?

sentences.native: رات جو ٿڌ ٿيندي، هيءَ چادر وٺو.
sentences.roman: rāti jo thadha thīndī, hīa chādara vaṭho.
sentences.en: It gets cold at night — take this sheet.

sentences.native: مون کي نئين جاءِ تي ننڊ نٿي اچي.
sentences.roman: moṃ khe naīṃ jāi te nanḍa nathī ache.
sentences.en: I can't sleep in a new place.

sentences.native: سياري ۾ رلي کان سواءِ ننڊ نٿي اچي.
sentences.roman: siyāre meṃ ralī khāṃ savāi nanḍa nathī ache.
sentences.en: In winter I can't sleep without a ralli.

sentences.native: هيءَ رلي امان پاڻ ٺاهي آهي.
sentences.roman: hīa ralī amāṃ pāṇa ṭhāhī āhe.
sentences.en: Mum made this ralli herself.

sentences.native: مون کي صبح جو ستين وڳي جاڳائجو.
sentences.roman: moṃ khe subuh jo satīṃ vaɠe jāɠāijo.
sentences.en: Please wake me at seven in the morning.

sentences.native: مون کي ڏاڍي ننڊ آئي، رلي ڏاڍي گرم هئي.
sentences.roman: moṃ khe ɗāḍhī nanḍa āī, ralī ɗāḍhī garamu huī.
sentences.en: I slept really well — the ralli was so warm.

tip.title: 'Used to' = -ndo + هو
tip.body:
- Take the -ndo form (as in the future) and add the past of 'be': مان ويندو **هوس** 'I used to go'.
- Both parts agree: هو ويندو **هو**، هوءَ ويندي **هئي**، اسين ويندا **هئاسين**، هو ويندا **هئا**.
- No ergative here: **مان** چانهه پيئندو هوس.

sentences.native: ننڍپڻ ۾ مان هر اونهاري ناني وٽ ويندو هوس.
sentences.roman: nanḍhapaṇa meṃ māṃ har unhāre nānī vaṭi vendo hos.
sentences.en: As a kid I used to go to my nani's every summer. (man)

sentences.native: اسين سڄو ڏينهن گهٽيءَ ۾ کيڏندا هئاسين.
sentences.roman: asīṃ saʄo ɗīṃhu ghiṭīa meṃ kheɗandā huāsīṃ.
sentences.en: We used to play in the street all day.

sentences.native: امان صبح جو سوير اٿندي هئي.
sentences.roman: amāṃ subuh jo sver uthandī huī.
sentences.en: Mum used to get up early in the morning.

sentences.native: اسان جا سڀ گهرڀاتي گڏ رهندا هئا.
sentences.roman: asāṃ jā sabhu gharbhātī gaɗu rahandā huā.
sentences.en: Our whole family used to live together.

sentences.native: توهان ڪٿي ڪم ڪندا هئا؟
sentences.roman: tavhāṃ kithe kamu kandā huā?
sentences.en: Where did you use to work?

sentences.native: ننڍپڻ ۾ اسين عيد تي ڳوٺ ويندا هئاسين.
sentences.roman: nanḍhapaṇa meṃ asīṃ ʿīda te ɠoṭha vendā huāsīṃ.
sentences.en: When we were kids we used to go to the village for Eid.

sentences.native: گهرڀاتي سڀ آچر تي گڏجي ماني کائيندا هئا.
sentences.roman: gharbhātī sabhu āchara te gaɗjī mānī khāīndā huā.
sentences.en: The whole family used to eat together on Sundays.

sentences.native: بابا کي رات جو دير سان ماني کائڻ جي عادت هئي.
sentences.roman: bābā khe rāti jo dera sāṃ mānī khāiṇa jī ʿādata huī.
sentences.en: Dad was in the habit of eating late at night.

sentences.native: مون کي دير سان اٿڻ جي عادت آهي.
sentences.roman: moṃ khe dera sāṃ uthaṇa jī ʿādata āhe.
sentences.en: I'm in the habit of getting up late.

tip.title: There used to be… / I didn't use to…
tip.body:
- 'There used to be' = **هوندو هو** (m) / **هوندي هئي** (f): اڳي هتي دڪان **هوندو هو**.
- Negative: **نه** before the verb: مان چانهه **نه** پيئندو هوس.
- A woman says **هيس** 'I was': مان ويندي **هيس**.

sentences.native: اڳي هن گهٽيءَ ۾ هڪ وڏو دڪان هوندو هو.
sentences.roman: aɠe hin ghiṭīa meṃ hiku vaɗo dukānu hundo ho.
sentences.en: There used to be a big shop on this street.

sentences.native: ڳوٺ ۾ هر وڏي گهر ۾ اوطاق هوندي هئي.
sentences.roman: ɠoṭha meṃ har vaɗe ghara meṃ otāqa hundī huī.
sentences.en: In the village every big house used to have an otaq.

sentences.native: مان اڳي چانهه نه پيئندو هوس، هاڻي روز پيئان ٿو.
sentences.roman: māṃ aɠe chānhi na pīndo hos, hāṇe roz pīāṃ tho.
sentences.en: I didn't use to drink tea — now I have it every day. (man)

sentences.native: ننڍپڻ ۾ مان امان سان رڌڻي ۾ ويهندي هيس.
sentences.roman: nanḍhapaṇa meṃ māṃ amāṃ sāṃ radhaṇe meṃ vehandī huyas.
sentences.en: As a girl I used to sit with Mum in the kitchen.

sentences.native: اڳي مهمان اوطاق ۾ ترسندا هئا.
sentences.roman: aɠe mehmāna otāqa meṃ tarsandā huā.
sentences.en: Guests used to stay in the otaq.

sentences.native: اسان وٽ رواج آهي ته مهمان پهريان کائي.
sentences.roman: asāṃ vaṭi riwāju āhe ta mehmānu pahiryāṃ khāe.
sentences.en: It's our custom that the guest eats first.

sentences.native: بابا اسان کي روز اسڪول ڇڏي ايندو هو.
sentences.roman: bābā asāṃ khe roz iskūla chhaɗī endo ho.
sentences.en: Dad used to drop us at school every day.

sentences.native: هي رواج اڳي ڳوٺن ۾ هوندو هو، هاڻي شهرن ۾ به آهي.
sentences.roman: hī riwāju aɠe ɠoṭhan meṃ hundo ho, hāṇe shaharan meṃ bi āhe.
sentences.en: This custom used to be in the villages — now it's in the cities too.

sentences.native: ايندڙ ڀيري اسان وٽ اچجو، امان به خوش ٿيندي.
sentences.roman: endaṛa bhere asāṃ vaṭi achijo, amāṃ bi xushu thīndī.
sentences.en: Come to ours next time — Mum will be happy too.
